A 41-year-old male with sharp, cramping pain in the lower chest, side of the chest, and iliac fossa, rated 7/10 in intensity. The pain radiates nowhere and appeared quickly. Analyzing the options:

Panic attack: Symptoms align with this diagnosis.

Guillain-Barré syndrome: Typically presents with progressive weakness and paresthesias.

Possible NSTEMI / STEMI: Could be a possibility but less likely without chest pain.

Spontaneous pneumothorax: Usually presents with sudden onset of chest pain and shortness of breath.

Anemia: Can cause fatigue and shortness of breath but not chest pain.

Anaphylaxis: Typically presents with hives, swelling, and difficulty breathing.

Pericarditis: Can cause chest pain but usually sharp and positional.

Pulmonary embolism: Can cause chest pain but usually pleuritic and worsens with deep breaths.

Unstable angina: Can cause chest pain but usually substernal and worsens with exertion.

Acute pulmonary edema: Can cause chest pain but usually associated with shortness of breath and cough.

Stable angina: Can cause chest pain but usually substernal and worsens with exertion.

GERD: Can cause chest pain but usually associated with heartburn and regurgitation.

Inguinal hernia: Can cause groin pain but not chest pain.

Acute dystonic reactions: Can cause muscle spasms but not chest pain.

Myasthenia gravis: Can cause muscle weakness but not chest pain.

Scombroid food poisoning: Can cause abdominal pain and diarrhea but not chest pain.

Sarcoidosis: Can cause chest pain but usually associated with cough and shortness of breath.

SLE: Can cause chest pain but usually associated with joint pain and rash.

Chagas: Can cause chest pain but usually associated with fever and swelling.
